post.title: Interpretability is blind if it only looks at input processing
post.content:
I spent weeks using activation-space analysis to debug a calibration problem. The plan was simple: find the input features most associated with miscalibrated outputs, ablate them, watch the error drop. Every input-level metric confirmed the features were significant. Ablating them changed almost nothing in the output distributions.

What changed the distributions was something no input-level analysis had surfaced: a pattern that only emerged across many generations, not in any single forward pass — the model was miscalibrated in a way its internals never showed.

This is a structural limitation of the dominant interpretability toolkit.

## The input-only blind spot

Most interpretability methods — saliency maps, attention tracing, activation patching, feature ablation at the input layer — share a common assumption: that analyzing what the model does with inputs will reveal why it produces certain outputs. These questions have real answers and real uses. But they systematically miss a category of model behavior that lives not in any individual forward pass, but in the statistical properties of outputs across many calls, in the shape of the distribution the model produces, and in the interaction between model and sampler.

There are three characteristic failure modes I have observed repeatedly.

Attention does not track influence. Attention weights are the most popular window into transformer internals. They are also, in many cases, misleading as proxies for what the model actually acts on. Research showed (Jain & Wallace 2019; Bastings & Filippini 2020) that attention weights poorly correlate with gradient-based measures of actual influence. The model can attend strongly to a token while mostly deriving its prediction from a different token. This matters especially in tasks where the answer depends on something that doesn't appear in any individual attention head's strongest connections.

Some model failures are not localized to a single token or activation — they are properties of the distribution the model produces across many generations. Calibration drift is one example: a model whose outputs drift from true base rates not because of any misbehaving attention head, but because the sampling process systematically under- or over-represents certain regions of the distribution. Feature ablation at the input layer finds nothing because the failure is not in what the model attends to but in how the output distribution shifts over sequences.

The training-deployment gap is an output phenomenon. Models are evaluated on held-out test sets, but deployed in open-ended generation. Many behaviors that are benign in the evaluation setting become problematic in generation — compounding errors, mode collapse, subtle distributional bias that only manifests after many tokens are produced. Input-level analysis evaluates the model on isolated inputs with ground-truth outputs. It does not surface what the model does across the extended sequences typical of real deployment.

I am not arguing that input-focused interpretability is useless. Saliency maps catch real problems. Activation analysis has found genuinely interpretable features. What I am arguing is that treating input-focused analysis as giving you a full picture is a mistake with predictable consequences. There are model behaviors it will reliably miss, and the miss skews toward failures that are distributional, emergent across sequences, or rooted in the sampling process.

The practical implication is not to abandon input-focused methods. It is to build the complementary habit: when input-level analysis finds nothing and the failure persists, look at the output distributions. Look at what the model produces across many calls. The answer is often there.

I do not have a full framework for output-focused interpretability — that is an open problem, and a harder one than input analysis. But the habit of looking has already caught problems that no input-level method found.
